mediaWork.title: Wrongful Conviction
mediaWork.publisherOrNetwork: Lava for Good, Signal Company Number One
mediaWork.focusOrTheme: Wrongful Convictions, Personal Narratives of Exonerees, Systemic Issues in the Justice System (Police/Prosecutorial Misconduct, Brady Violations), Legal Advocacy, Prison Reform Programs.

mediaItem.focusOrTheme: Wrongful Conviction of Jermaine Archer, Brady violation, eyewitness testimony, prosecutorial misconduct.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction details the story of Jermaine Archer, wrongfully convicted for a 1997 murder in Brooklyn, New York. The conviction heavily relied on the shifting testimony of Carlos Bethune... Jermaine is now paroled but continues to fight for full exoneration.
mediaItem.keyQuotes:
Jermaine: "When you lock up the wrong person, the right person remains free and everybody's in danger."
Jermaine: (Recounting interaction with detective) "And I remember saying something slick like, 'The jacket don't fit'... And as if we had both seen the same movie, he spent right back. 'I know a good tailor.'"
Jermaine: (On jury deliberation) "One of the jurors reached out to my brother after the trial... and said [she] couldn't get over the nickname 'Bang'."
Jermaine: (Recounting off-the-record judge comment to ADA Peggy Hoffman) "You're over trying this case. He's clearly not an angel, but it doesn't look like he did this." ADA Hoffman's alleged reply: "I'm just following instructions from up top..."
Jermaine: (Regarding his time in prison) "I realized my time was the same whether I was in prison or not because it mattered when I hit that grave that tombstone that dash all of this time count."
Jermaine: (On the goal of Voices from Within) "They don't care how much you know, they want to know how much you care. And we actually show them that we care about you."
Jermaine's final call to action: "Contact the district attorney [Kings County] and ask them where's the evidence that I did this crime... Find out why he has me in this scope and why he won't do the right thing."

individuals.sentence: Not explicitly stated, but resulted in 22 years served before parole.
individuals.narrativeSummary: Wrongfully convicted for a 1997 murder in Brooklyn, New York. Conviction overturned in 2023 due to Brady violation. Served 22 years. Paroled in 2020. Continues to fight for full exoneration.
